## **Careers**
## The Children of Grungni
## **Character Creation**
Dwarf character creation is covered in the _**WFRP Rulebook**_ (pages 38-41). Players are encouraged to work with the Gamemaster to develop interesting backgrounds for their Character. A Character’s background should be fleshed out with such details as parents, siblings, and other close family members (including spouse and children, if applicable) by name. 

Gamemasters (with Players input) should consider adding descriptions of events that led the Character to give up a relatively comfortable life to go on the road. Such detail should seed adventure hooks that a Gamemaster could use in some capacity later in the campaign. 

The following section contains useful tools and table to flesh out your Dwarf ’s background. 

## **Dwarf Names**
Dwarf names consist of three elements: the forename or personal name, the surname, and the clan name. Dwarf etiquette governs the use of names. For practical purposes, the more formal the situation, the individual’s full name and guild standing will be used. 

For example, Master Brewer Breda Roreksdottir of Clan Oakbarrel would be the full name and title of the Dragonbreath Tavern owner in the Neiderwind district of Altdorf. Her full name would be used in a guild (or hold, if she was a Karak Dwarf) ceremony. Those addressing her in other settings would use different names depending on their relative status. Dwarf superiors in the Brewers Guild (since she is an Imperial Dwarf) would call her Breda Roreksdottir while Dwarf equals and inferiors would use Master Breda. 

Dwarfs from outside the Brewers Guild would refer to her as Master Brewer Breda. When talking about her in the third person, Breda’s surname is used. 

Family members will generally refer to each other according to their relationship, so Breda’s family might refer to her as _Kuni_ (Cousin) or _Nez_ (Niece). 

## **Naming Rites**
Dwarf forenames (or given names) tend to be short, usually one or two syllables. Some names may reflect traditional names handed down from one generation to another, while others commemorate a venerated clan ancestor or great hero. As an example of the latter, generations after the War of Vengeance, many newborn males were given the name of Gotrek after the victorious High King who put an end to the insufferable Phoenix King of Ulthuan. A few given names reflect virtues that parents hope their offspring will emulate. Gorm is often associated with wisdom, Grim with prowess in battle, and Dwinbar with skill at craftsmanship. 

## **Surnames**
Dwarf surnames are based on the name of the person who raised them. In families where a father is present (since death rates among Dwarf men tend to be higher as more of them go to war than women), the children take on the father’s name with the suffix of either ‘ _sson_ ’ for males or ‘ _sdottir_ ’ for daughters. If the father perished when the child is very young, then the young Dwarf takes on the mother’s name with the appropriate suffix. Dwarfs retain the widowed mother’s name even if she later remarries. Dwarfs who lose both parents early in life will take on the name of the aunt or uncle who raised them with the suffix of either ‘ _snev_ ’ (nephew of) or ‘ _sniz_ ’ (niece of).

The formal surname of ‘Khazadsson’ or ‘Khazadsdottir’ is used in the extremely rare occurrences where a newborn Dwarf is a foundling of unknown descent. Once the foundling is adopted by another Dwarf, the youngling adds another name consisting of the foster parent’s name with the suffix ‘ _sfind_ ’ (found by).  For example, the foundling Dwarf named Grim and raised by Kazran Moreksson would be Grim Khazadsson-Kazransfind. 

When they come of age, Imperial Dwarf foundlings may opt to petition the elders of their adopted clan to change their surname. Usually, these foundlings replace their adopted surname with the (Reikspiel equivalent of) their clan name. In extremely rare cases, Imperial Dwarf clans may decide to go it alone without a surname until they can earn a surname through deed or achievement. 

## **Nicknames**
A fair number of Dwarfs also have nicknames. These are derived from outstanding deeds, personality quirks, or distinguished physical features. In less formal settings, these nicknames sometimes replace a Dwarf ’s actual surname.  For example, Brokk Furgilsson earned his nickname ‘Burned-Thumb’ from the time the apprentice picked up a still-hot, recently-cast blank brooch. Dwarfs may not choose their own nickname. It must be bestowed upon them by a Master of a Craftguild or Clan consensus. Dwarfs must take great care to avoid gaining an unflattering nickname. 

Those bestowing nicknames also must take care that the conferred nickname accurately represents a true characteristic or deed of the Dwarf in question. Granting an inaccurate nickname reflects poorly on the bestower and may be considered an insult to the Dwarf or clan. Such insults would need to be answered. 

Nicknames are not fixed in stone like their other names. As Dwarfs age and accrue deeds, one nickname may get replaced by a new, more accurate one. For example, Brokk Burned-Thumb might slay Orc Warboss Gronk in battle years later and become Brokk Grontslayer in honour of his great deed. Still later, Brokk may lose an eye fighting against a (rather lucky) Goblin. He would then become Brokk Scar-Eyed. 

Nicknames must be as unique as possible. Advocating for the same nickname as an older Dwarf, especially a great king or hero, is presumptuous and an insult to the original bearer of the nickname. The only acceptable way this could be done is if it is the original bearer of the nickname bestowing it upon the younger Dwarf. 

Few nicknames do not require the approval of a Craftguild Master or consensus of an Elder Council. Suitors may give nicknames that flatter their intended’s achievements, appearance or temperament. Nicknames such as ‘the Fair’ or ‘the Beautiful’ have been over-used in recent centuries and fallen out of favour. Nicknames such as ‘Ravenhair’, ‘Emerald-Eyes’, and ‘Radiant Smile’ are still popular among suitors. It is a sign of great favour when the intended accepts the nickname given by a suitor. 

## **Clan Names**
Dwarf clan names are rarely used outside Dwarf society. Clan names were originally established early in Dwarf culture from the nickname of the clan’s founding ancestor. These names generally remain unchanged for millennia. For example, the Dwarfkings of Karak Ungor derived their clan name of Stonehammer ( _Durazgrund_ ) from the nickname of their ancestor, Grum Stonehammer. Grum went to battle with a massive stone hammer during the Coming of Chaos wars, taking great pleasure in cracking the skulls of his enemies. The stone hammer was reputed to be so heavy that the only other Dwarf who could wield it was the Ancestor God, Grimnir. Though the weapon was lost in the fall of Karak Ungor, the clan continued to carry the name ‘Stonehammers’ to the present. 

In the rare times friction within a clan cannot be peacefully resolved, Clan Elders may deny the offending faction the right to use the clan’s name. The elders of the now splintered fraction then meet to determine the clan’s name going forward. The new name must be petitioned through the dwarf hold’s Elder Loremaster to ensure the new Clan name is not already in use in the hold or elsewhere. The faction removed from the clan oftentimes depart the Dwarf hold or settlement and move elsewhere. 

Within Dwarf society, the clan name is always expressed in Khazalid. Within the Empire, the clan name (if used) is always expressed in Reikspiel. 

Some Imperial Dwarfs engage in work that could prove embarrassing for the clan, such as helping mass produce inexpensive tools or weapons as part of a Human industry. In these cases, Imperial Dwarfs may abandon their clan name in favour of a nonsense one to protect the reputation of the clan as well as forestall any reprisal. For example, when Rogue Engineer Kragg Grimsson departed the Dwarf Engineers Guild in Nuln over an argument with the Master Engineer, Kragg adopted the clan name of ‘No-Name’ ( _Nanavn_ ) so that work he does for Grand Duchess in Talabheim does not reflect poorly on his former clan of _Azrilbar_ (‘Silvery Gate’). 

## **Place of Origin**
Gamemasters may decide without input from where a Dwarf Character hails when considering the needs of the campaign. Gamemasters might also opt to negotiate such as a decision with the Player of a Dwarf character. 

At times, it can be more entertaining to randomly choose where a Dwarf Character originated and then use that to determine the Character’s back story.

## **Physical Attributes**
Determining physical attributes is also important in developing a Dwarf Character. The following table expands on the information in the _**WFRP Rulebook**_ (pages 40). 

Dwarfs have a wide distribution along the Mountains from ranging from Dwarf holds overlooking the arid and Greenskin-infested Badlands to those enduring the cold winds of Norsca. Traits such as hair and eye colour differ between these far-flung lands. 

As most Dwarf Characters would come from lands between these extremes, there is a reasonable distribution of such traits. For Norse Dwarf Characters, subtract 5% from each of the dice rolls for hair and eye colour. For Dwarf Characters from the Vaults, Black Mountains, Tilea, and southern Worlds Edge Mountains add 5 to the dice rolls. 

The optional column for Distinguished Features does not require a modified roll. This roll is intended to give a Dwarf Character a distinguishing attribute to help the Character stand out (and, perhaps, provide a basis for a nickname). Dwarf Characters should have no more than one of these features, but the Game Master may allow more in order to create an interesting Character. 

## **Dwarf Language**
The Dwarf language is called Khazalid. Although it has adopted few words from interactions with other cultures, Khazalid has remained remarkably unchanged compared to any other Old World language. In fact, Khazalid has had more influence on other languages than they have had on it. Many words in Reikspiel and Norse derive from the Dwarfen tongue from trading and other interactions over the course of millennia. Even the debased and vile Dark Tongue and foul-sounding guttural Orc languages have words with Khazalid elements. 

## **Khazalid**
Among Dwarfs, Khazalid is spoken freely. It is rarely heard by others, except for the war cries and curses emanating from the field of battle. The Dwarfs are so secretive about their language that they never speak in their tongue when in the presence of others. Additionally, Dwarfs never teach their language to outsiders. What little manlings have gleaned of Khazalid comes from Verenan scholars, researchers, and historians. 

Most Dwarf words have several meanings. One must consider the context in which it is used to understand the exact meaning of a Khazalid word. The way a word ends (the signifier) can also help determine its meaning, though the rules regarding this are not absolute. 

The Dwarf runic script is extremely ancient, dating back to the time during their early history when  they expanded out from the south of the Worlds Edge Mountains. Their distinctive angular form resulted from the hard materials (wood, metal, and stone) upon which the Dwarfs inscribed them with a knife or chisel. Even today, Dwarfs prefer to inscribe their books on long, thin scrolls of beaten metal (such as gold or copper) instead of parchment. Occasionally leather is used when metal is scarce. The great sacred tomes of Karaz-a-Karak, the Book of Remembering and the Great Book of Grudges, are written on thousands of sheets of gold (or goldcopper alloy) beaten as thin as parchment. 

The runic script includes a basic alphabet ( _Klinkarhun_ ) and pictographic characters. Both kinds of runes can be found mixed in Khazalid texts from the Golden Age. Older pictorial runes did not fall entirely out of common use until a few hundred years before the migration of the warlike manling tribes ( _Unberogens_ , for example) migrated into the lands now known as the Empire. Secret and ancient texts from the Long Migration and Age of Ancestor Gods tend to be written exclusively with picture runes. Text and records from the time since the manlings spread throughout the Old World are exclusively written in basic alphabetic runes. 

Dwarfs do not have any runes or words for distinguishing between the sexes. Dwarfs do not concern themselves with an individual’s gender, but rather their abilities, skills, and reputation. The sole exceptions to this rule involve the rune denoting the King’s consort and certain familial relationships. 

Khazalid texts are written and maintained by the Runescribe craftguild. Clan members of certain craftguilds also know how to read and write alphabetic rune texts. Still, a great deal of daily life does not require writing at all. Many ordinary clan Dwarfs are functionally illiterate, although most can tell the difference between an alphabetic rune and magical runes (and thus can identify runic artefacts without understanding the properties). They can also recognise basic words such as a personal name or simple texts used in day to day trading. 

The Norse Dwarf dialect is slightly different from the version of Khazalid used by the Karak and Imperial Dwarfs. Nonetheless, any of the Dwarf kindred can be understood by another. 

## **Khazalid Glossary**
The following table offers a sample of Khazalid words and their equivalence in the manling tongue. Gamemasters and Players of Dwarf Characters are advised to use Khazalid words sparingly. It is a secret language and any Dwarf teaching these words to manling, Elf, or any other non-Dwarf Characters will be considered in violation of Dwarf Law for treason (a capital crime).

## Dwarf Origins
This section provides rules for Dwarfs from different homelands, and a new random Class and Career table that incorporates the new Careers in this book. If creating a Dwarf Character from a smaller hold not listed here, use the rules for an Imperial Dwarf, which is an all-round flexible choice for Dwarfs far from the influence of major Karaks. 

## **Dwarfs (Karaz-A-Karak)**
All that is most glorious about the Everlasting Realm can be found in the Dwarf capital of Karaz-a-Karak. Adventurers from the Everpeak act as self-appointed representatives of the High King himself, binding themselves to his vow to right every wrong in the Great Book of Grudges. 

**Skills** : Consume Alcohol, Cool, Endurance, Entertain (Storytelling), Evaluate, Language (Khazalid), Leadership, Lore (Dwarfs), Lore (Geology), Lore (Metallurgy), Melee (Basic), Trade (Any One) 

**Talents** : Ancestral Grudge* _or_ Resolute, Magic Resistance, Night Vision, Read/Write _or_ Relentless, Sturdy 

## **Dwarfs (Barak Varr)**
The home of the Dwarf navy is based in the Border Princes, a rare beacon of stability amongst lawless Human kingdoms. Its people trade extensively with the neighbouring principalities, and are generally more welcoming and curious about the outside world. 

**Skills** : Consume Alcohol, Cool, Endurance, Entertain (Storytelling), Evaluate, Haggle, Language (Khazalid), Lore (Dwarfs), Melee (Basic), Navigation, Sail, Trade (Any One) 

**Talents** : Dealmaker _or_ Strong-minded, Magic Resistance, Night Vision, Read/Write _or_ Resolute,  Sturdy 

## **Dwarfs (Karak Azul)**
The weapon-smithies of Karak Azul have become a dark and joyless place since the kidnapping of King Kazador’s kin by the Orc warlord Gorfang Rotgut. A king’s ransom has been promised to the adventurers that return the captured kin from Black Crag, and slay the monster Gorfang. 

**Skills** : Climb, Consume Alcohol, Cool, Endurance, Evaluate, Haggle, Intimidate, Language (Khazalid), Lore (Dwarfs), Lore (Metallurgy), Melee (Basic), Trade (Any One) 

**Talents** : Hatred (Orcs and Goblins) _or_ Resolute, Magic Resistance, Night Vision, Read/Write _or_ Relentless, Sturdy 

## **Dwarfs (Karak Eight Peaks)**
Karak Eight Peaks is an active warzone, as King Belegar’s kin fight an endless siege to liberate the occupied hold. Clansfolk are rarely permitted to leave the front, but adventurous Dwarfs may be dispatched abroad to find weapons, allies, or information that can help wage the war at home. 

**Skills** : Consume Alcohol, Cool, Endurance, Evaluate, Intuition, Language (Khazalid), Lore (Dwarfs), Lore (Geology), Lore (Warfare), Melee (Basic), Set Traps, Trade (Any One) 

**Talents** : Magic Resistance, Night Vision, Read/Write _or_ Resolute, Strong-minded _or_ Tenacious, Sturdy 

## **Dwarfs (Karak Kadrin)**
The Slayer’s Keep is the centre of worship for Grimnir, the Dwarf god of war. Many warriors live and die here, battling to control the critical Peak Pass connecting the Old World to the far east. For others, it is just as the first step of their journey, to seek glorious combat wherever it is found. 

**Skills** : Consume Alcohol, Cool, Endurance, Entertain (Storytelling), Evaluate, Gamble, Intimidate, Language (Khazalid), Lore (Dwarfs), Lore (Metallurgy), Melee (Basic), Trade (Any One) 

**Talents** : Iron Jaw _or_ Read/Write, Magic Resistance, Night Vision, Resolute _or_ Strong-minded, Sturdy 

## **Dwarfs (Zhufbar)**
Zhufbar is the main hub of Dwarf industry, and the centre of the Engineering Guild. The Karak is always at the forefront of technical innovation, with greater acceptance of new ideas than is found in other holds. Field tests of new inventions often carry its inhabitants far from home. 

**Skills** : Consume Alcohol, Cool, Endurance, Entertain (Storytelling), Evaluate, Language (Khazalid), Lore (Dwarfs), Lore (Engineering), Lore (Geology), Lore (Metallurgy), Melee (Basic), Trade (Any One) 

**Talents** : Magic Resistance, Night Vision, Read/Write _or_ Relentless, Strong-minded _or_ Tinker, Sturdy 

## Dwarfs (Karak Hirn/black Mountains)
Much travel through the Black Mountains is conducted overland, and adventurous Dwarfs in the region are as comfortable scrabbling up mountainsides as delving into Goblin tunnels. Foremost amongst this range is Karak Hirn, the Hornhold, which exploits the natural acoustics of their surrounding canyons to signal the outside world. 

**Skills** : Consume Alcohol, Climb, Cool, Endurance, Entertain (Storytelling), Evaluate, Haggle, Language (Khazalid), Lore (Dwarfs), Melee (Basic), Play (Horn), Trade (Any One) 

**Talents** : Magic Resistance, Night Vision, Read/Write _or_ Relentless, Scale Sheer Surface _or_ Strong-minded, Sturdy 

## **Dwarfs (Karak Izor/the Vaults)**
The Vaults were the first ranges settled by Dwarfs outside the World’s Edge Mountains, with Karak Izor its centre of defence. Whilst most Dwarfs have abandoned the subterranean tunnels of the Karaz Ankor as unsafe, the Dwarfs of Karak Izor labour underground extensively, constructing their own Underway. 

**Skills** : Consume Alcohol, Climb, Cool, Endurance, Entertain (Storytelling), Evaluate, Language (Khazalid), Lore (Dwarfs), Lore (Geology), Melee (Basic), Outdoor Survival, Trade (Any One) 

**Talents** : Enclosed Fighter _or_ Resolute, Magic Resistance, Night Vision, Read/Write _or_ Relentless, Sturdy 

## Dwarfs (Karak Norn/grey Mountains)
The holds of the Grey Mountains were never prosperous, and their inhabitants learned long ago how to persist in lean times. Many have abandoned their holds to seek opportunity elsewhere. In Karak Norn, distrust of the Wood Elves in Athel Loren rarely abates, and missions to surveil the devious Elves are often led astray. 

**Skills** : Consume Alcohol, Climb, Cool, Endurance, Entertain (Storytelling), Evaluate, Language (Khazalid), Lore (Dwarfs), Melee (Basic), Perception, Ranged (Crossbow), Trade (Any One) 

**Talents** : Magic Resistance, Night Vision, Read/Write _or_ Relentless, Resolute _or_ Stone Soup, Sturdy 

## **Dwarfs (Norse)**
The Dwarfs of the frozen north are hearty and independent. After centuries of isolation, they are keen to explore the wider world, by exercising the naval expertise they gleaned from cultural exchange with Human tribes. Even by Dwarf standards, their drinking binges are legendary. 

**Skills** : Climb, Consume Alcohol, Cool, Endurance, Entertain (Storytelling), Evaluate, Language (Khazalid), Language (Norse), Lore (Dwarfs), Melee (Basic), Sail, Trade (Any One) 

**Talents** : Carouser _or_ Strong-minded, Magic Resistance, Night Vision, Read/Write _or_ Relentless, Sturdy 

## **Dwarfs (Imperial)**
The reign of Sigmar, Wars of the Vampire Counts, and Great War Against Chaos were all succeeded by waves of Dwarfen expatriation in the Empire. Their numbers are periodically swelled by Karak exiles, and refugees from fallen holds. Though often disparaged by their mountaintop cousins, Imperial Dwarfs emulate both the traditional customs of Karaz Ankor, and the manling tendency to seek glory through adventure. 

**Skills** : Consume Alcohol, Cool, Endurance, Entertain (Storytelling), Evaluate, Intimidate, Language (Khazalid), Lore (Dwarfs), Lore (Geology), Lore (Metallurgy), Melee (Basic), Trade (Any One) 

**Talents** : Magic Resistance, Night Vision, Read/Write _or_ Relentless, Resolute _or_ Strong-minded, Sturdy 

## **Longbeards**
Most Dwarf adventurers are relatively young, with few retaining their wanderlust and curiosity beyond their first century of life. But circumstances may conspire for an older Dwarf to set off on their own adventures — be that undertaking a quest, serving in a military campaign, or seeking restitution for a long-standing grudge. 

At the GM’s discretion, a player generating a Dwarf Character may choose to play a Longbeard, instead of using the usual age range detailed in **WFRP Core Rulebook** . The Character immediately reduces their Fate and Fortune scores by 1. If the Character has 0 Fate, they instead reduce their Resilience and Resolve scores by 1. 

Longbeards have a good 120 years or more of life experience, and are afforded great prestige in Dwarf society. When interacting with other Dwarfs, Longbeards in the Brass or Silver Tier ( **WFRP Core Rulebook** ) count their Status as Gold 1, whilst Longbeards in the Gold Tier count their Standing as 1 higher. This modified Status affects what modifiers apply to social Skill Tests, but is not used whilst Earning. See page 133 for more detail about how Dwarfs view their elders. 

In addition, Longbeards are notoriously stubborn, resistant to any person, monster, disease, or inanimate object that tries to tell them what to do. They gain +10 on all Tests to avoid gaining a Condition, and on Tests to remove any Conditions they already have. 

During play, if a Dwarf Character is rewarded a Fate point to mark the completion of a long adventure or arc, they may choose to forgo the Fate point to become a Longbeard instead, if their Character is of suitable age. This is most appropriate if there is a significant time break before the start of the next adventure.

## **Lustrian Adventures**
If you have a copy of **Lustria** , and expect your Dwarf to be exploring a hazardous locale, you can use the new careers in that supplement by replacing some results on the Dwarf Random Class and Career Table. Specifically, you can choose to play an Interpreter instead of a Lawyer; a Trailblazer instead of a Coachman; or a Survivalist instead of a Pedlar (an exception to the usual rule that Survivalists are replacements for Road Wardens). 

## **Dwarfs at Sea**
Dwarfs are not natural sailors, but if forced to adapt to maritime living, they approach it with the same rugged determination that they approach everything else. If you have a copy of **Sea of Claws** , you may choose to use the careers included for the Seafarer Class, by replacing some results on the Dwarf Random Class and Career Table (instead of using the table on **Sea of Claws** page 63): 

- The Huffer and Wrecker can be replaced with their Seafarer counterparts. 

- The Boatman can be replaced with the Officer. 

- The Riverwoman and Seaman can be replaced with the Sailor. 

- The Smuggler and Stevedore can be replaced with the Ship’s Gunner. 

## Careers
_‘What you want in life, beardling, is a proper vocation. What are you here for other than to produce, at the end of the day? Work hard and earn your rewards. Put food on the table, gold in the trove, and ale in your belly. Don’t faff about like some feckless Elgi, wasting your long life on frippery, nor dash about all slipshod like a lickspittle manling. Ah, I hardly blame the Umgi really, they don’t live long enough to get good at anything.’_ 

— Grognibald Oldhammer, disgruntled Longbeard 

## **Not a Proper Dwarf**
Like any society, the Karaks have a mostly-unwritten code of conduct, and expectations about how “proper” Dwarfs are supposed to behave. These customs have been detailed throughout this book, to provide players and Gamemasters with useful prompts for how to roleplay as a respectable Dwarf. However, there will always be exceptional Dwarfs within the Karaks who persist in flouting these conventions, refusing to conform to the role expected of their age, gender, bloodline, etc. These rebels are bound to cause trouble, often becoming outcasts, runaways, or self-imposed exiles. In other words, they are exactly the kind of itinerant misfit that is most appropriate for a **WFRP** player Character. 

This is to say that the guidelines provided for how to act as a Dwarf Character are just that: guidelines. They aren’t a script to follow as you play, or a checklist that automates how every Dwarf responds to every situation. Dwarfs are people, with their own unique personalities and perspectives, who do not always live up to the staunch expectations of their ancestors (even when they try). Roleplay your Dwarf Character in that spirit, and you’ll avoid robbing yourself of the opportunity to discover who they are in play — perhaps even surprising yourself. 

## **Dwarf Career Updates**
This section includes updates to the core Careers in **Warhammer Fantasy Roleplay** , which apply when a Dwarf Character enters that Career. It includes new Career levels to replace levels in the original Career, to reflect the unique way in which Dwarfs practise that Career. These alternate Career levels are optional — Dwarf Characters can still use the levels printed in **WFRP** if they choose, or even pay the usual XP cost to Change to a New Level ( **WFRP Core Rulebook** ) and acquire both the original and alternate versions of that Career level. Unless otherwise stated, alternate Career levels have the same corresponding Characteristic as the Career level they replace. 

**Example** : _Kala has completed her Student Engineer Career, and is Changing to a New Level. She could choose to become an Engineer (_ **WFRP Core Rulebook** _) or Guild Engineer (page 56), both the second level of her current Career. Either way, the new Characteristic she can purchase Advances for is Initiative._ 

_Later, Kala completes the second level of her Career as a Guild Engineer, and Changes to a New Level again. She could become a Master Engineer, Outcast Engineer, Pilot, or even an Engineer (since she skipped that level to become a Guild Engineer). She chooses to become a Pilot — per the rules for that Career level, she can now buy Advances for the Agility Characteristic, but not Toughness._ 

## **Reading New Careers**
The Careers in this book use a mix of Talents from **WFRP** and from the new Talents list on pages 80-83. For ease of reference, Talents which are new to this book are denoted with an asterisk (*). 

The new Careers also denote some Trappings in italics. These indicate that the Trappings are required for a Character to perform their Career to minimum standard of quality. If a Character’s Required Trappings are lost or destroyed, the Character is ineligible to Earn Money until they are recovered, repaired, or repurchased. A Character without their Required Trappings may even be forced to change to a lower Career level, at the GM’s discretion. 

## **Dwarf Trappings**
## **Dwarf Rogues**
Dwarfs are notoriously proud of their wargear, ensuring that it is of the highest quality and embellished in accordance with their clan’s wealth. Dwarfs prefer the dependable surety of thick steel, shields, sturdy weapons, and thundering missile volleys to the duelling sabre, longbow, or unreliable minds of animal steeds. As such, many of the Trappings awarded as part of a Career may not be appropriate for a Dwarf Character. 

Any Dwarf Character that receives a Hand Weapon as a _or_ a Career Trapping may replace it with a Dwarf Axe Dwarf Warhammer. 

Any Dwarf Character that receives a Cavalry, Fencing, or Parry weapon as a Career Trapping may replace it with a Shield _or_ a Pistol with ammunition. 

Any Dwarf Character that receives a Bow Weapon as a Career Trapping may replace the weapon and its ammunition with a Dwarf Crossbow and ammunition _or_ a Dwarf Handgun and ammunition. 

Any Dwarf Character that receives a Riding Horse or Warhorse as a Career Trapping may replace it with Full Plate Armour and a Helm. 

Dwarfs that criminally profit from the hard work of their fellow clansfolk do not last long in the Karaks. A life of crime is anathema to the tenets of oath-keeping, honest labour, community spirit, and obedience of elders that all clans teach their beardlings from a young age. 

That said, whilst Dwarfs place a high value on the legal traditions of their ancestors, they are far less minded to observe the corrupt, byzantine, unjust legal systems of the Empire and other nations. It is therefore not uncommon for Dwarfs working abroad to be labelled as criminals. A Dwarf can be branded a Thief for retaking stolen treasures; a Fence for returning those treasures to rightful owners; an Outlaw for soliciting mountain “tolls” not approved by local authorities; or a Racketeer for using force to collect outstanding debts. 

When a Dwarf Character acquires the _Criminal_ Talent, they can choose whether its effects apply whilst visiting Dwarf settlements. If not, the Character does not generate increased Income when Earning money in Dwarf settlements, but also avoids the increased scrutiny of its occupants (which can be extremely hostile). 

A Dwarf Character may also choose to exchange their Career’s weapon Skill Specialisations to match the alternate Trapping options above — for example, a Dwarf Hunter could take Ranged (Crossbow _or_ Blackpowder) as a Career Skill instead of Ranged (Bow). 

## **Common Folk**
The greater part of any society’s population consists not of warriors and warlords, but civilian workers and their dependants. Dwarf Karaks are no different. 

Karak Townsfolk and other Burghers dwell within the heart of the mountains. Though most Dwarfs work some trade or another, service work is still important (if less prestigious): innkeepers, shopworkers, bartenders, and beard groomers can all make a decent living in the Karaks. Every craftsguild depends on Merchant kin to sell their wares, often to the Empire, where there is constant demand for high-quality Dwarf goods. 

Karak Villagers and other Peasants live at the outer peripheries of the mountain holds. At one extreme are the lowest deeps of the hold’s mine faces, an honourable place for Dwarfs to ply their trade. At the other extreme are the clans that labour above-ground: herdmasters, lumberjacks, trappers, and foragers. These clans seldom command much respect, as it is often claimed in the Karaks that overexposure to the sun has a deteriorative effect on the Dwarf psyche. 

## **Dwarf Engineer**
The Dwarf Engineers Guild trains the most technicallygifted minds in the Old World, and is forever the envy of the Imperial Engineers School. These geniuses are mostly content to reproduce the masterworks of their engineering ancestors, with true innovation the reserve of a maverick few. 

## **Guild Engineer**
War machines are a staple of Dwarfen throngs, and Guild Engineers train not just to assemble these devices, but accompany them into battle. Between campaigns, they assemble and supervise the industry of the Karaks, like water pumps, steam engines, and mining drills. 

Guild Engineers replace the 2nd level of the Engineer ( **WFRP Core Rulebook** ) or Artillerist ( **Up In Arms** page 18) Career. 

## **Sky Pilot**
Gyrocopters and other skycraft are still distrusted by the Guild’s elders, but many of the most daring Engineers are experts at maintaining and piloting them. Even the most disapproving Dwarf generals can appreciate the tactical advantage of reconnaissance from a bird’s eye view. 

Sky Pilots replace the 3rd level of the Engineer ( **WFRP Core Rulebook** ) Career. They replace their Career level’s corresponding Characteristic with Agility. 

## **Sky Pilot — Silver 3**
**Skills** : Charm, Navigation, Outdoor Survival, Sail (Skycraft) 

**Talents** : Acute Sense (Sight), Maverick*, Seasoned Traveller, Short Fuse* 

**Trappings** : _Pilot’s Licence_ , Dwarf Pistol, Telescope 

## **Guild Engineer — Silver 3**
**Skills** : Dodge, Drive, Melee (Any One), Ranged (Any One), Research, Trade (Any One) 

**Talents** : Craftsman (Engineer), Crew Commander*, Entrenchment*, Orientation 

**Trappings** : _Trade Tools (Engineer)_ , Dwarf Hammer _or_ Dwarf Greathammer, Dwarf Handgun _or_ Dwarf Pistol, Gromril Suit, Telescope 

## **Outcast Engineer**
Those who challenge the Engineers Guild’s hidebound conservatism are fated to undergo an elaborate exiling ritual. Despite the shame, many still practise their calling independently. Some even earn their way back into the Guild, though most inventors are only vindicated long after their death. 

Outcast Engineers replace the 3rd level of the Engineer ( **WFRP Core Rulebook** ) or Artillerist ( **Up In Arms** page 18) Career. They replace their Career level’s corresponding Characteristic with Fellowship. 

**Outcast Engineer — Silver 3 Skills** : Bribery, Entertain, Gamble, Trade (Any One) **Talents** : Argumentative, Dragon Belcher*, Master Tradesman (Engineer), Sniper **Trappings** : Dwarf Axe _or_ Dwarf Greataxe, Repeating Dwarf Handgun, Mark of Shame 

## **Dwarf Lawyer**
Dwarf law, like so much else in Dwarf culture, revolves around the recording and settling of grudges. For more detail see page 84. 

## **Dwarf Artisan**
Metalworkers, jewellers, weaponsmiths, and other craftsworkers are highly respected in Dwarf society, with stonemasons perhaps the most valued of all. For Brewers, see page 62. 

## **Reckoner**
Reckoners are intermediaries who carry records of outstanding grudges between clans and holds. Where possible, they negotiate settlements on their clients’ behalf, expunging grudges for later ratification. Traditionally their logs are inscribed on stone tablets, and shattered upon resolution. 

Reckoners replace the 2nd level of the Lawyer ( **WFRP Core Rulebook** ) Career. 

## **Reckoner — Silver 4**
**Skills** : Athletics, Evaluate, Intimidate, Lore (Heraldry _or_ History), Navigation, Stealth (Underground) **Talents** : Dealmaker, Menacing, Sturdy, Tireless* **Trappings** : _Reckoner’s Log_ , 1d10 Shattered Tablets, Runescribing Kit, Dwarf Axe _or_ Dwarf Hammer, Breastplate, Mail Skirt, Plate Helm (Open) 

## **Grudgemaster**
Sometimes known as Grudgekeepers, these scholars are the ultimate authorities on grudges and proportionate restitution, per the precedent set by revered ancestors. They may dictate the wording of grudges for their Kings to inscribe, or even be empowered to update their Karak’s Book of Grudges personally. 

Grudgemasters replace the 3rd level of the Lawyer ( **WFRP Core Rulebook** ) Career. 

## **Grudgemaster — Gold 1**
**Skills** : Intuition, Language (Any One), Lore (Any One), Secret Signs (Guilder) 

**Talents** : Ancestral Grudge*, Bookish, Long Memory*, Supportive **Trappings** : Research Archive, Beardling Apprentice, Key to the Hall of Remembering 

## **Stoneshaper**
Stoneshapers are a combination of mason, architect, and combat engineer, specialising in the construction of stone fortifications. They often supervise excavation work, as they are famed for their instinctive ability to anticipate rockfalls, earthquakes, and other underground disasters. Stoneshapers replace the 2nd level of the Artisan ( **WFRP Core Rulebook** ) Career. They replace their Career level’s corresponding Characteristic with Initiative. 

## **Stoneshaper — Silver 1**
**Skills** : Climb, Language (Guilder), Lore (Geology), Navigation, Set Trap, Stealth (Underground) **Talents** : Enclosed Fighter, Entrenchment*, Sixth Sense, Tireless* 

**Trappings** : _Trade Tools (Mason)_ , Dwarf Hammer 

## **Dwarf Artforms**
There is no truth to the Elven slander that Dwarfs cannot appreciate beauty — though it’s fair to say that what they consider appealing is different from most other cultures. Dwarf Art is an intensely physical process, requiring more strength than is usually expected from Artists. Sculpture is the most popular art form, but engraving and beard weaving are also regarded. Painting, in contrast, is dismissed as a trivial vanity. Dwarfs Entertain each other with work and, drinking songs, and long (often rambling) poetic sagas. Contrary to popular belief, Dwarfs do have a sense of humour — though it manifests as dry, sardonic remarks on matters that others might find grave and serious, stoic acknowledgement of disasters when others around them are panicking, begrudging admiration of things others find aweinspiring, and boisterous, competitive boasting when others would prefer things to be civil. 

The Perform Skill is seldom used by Dwarfs, as they are more impressed by feats of endurance than agility: ox lifting, stone hauling, anvil heaving, and bellowing. Some beardlings practise juggling with crafting tools, though they are encouraged to abandon such frivolity by their elders, and treat their labours with the seriousness it deserves. Though Dwarfs Play all kinds of musical instruments, the most popular are those that echo far through their mountain holds: driving percussion and sonorous horns. The largest horns are sometimes used to communicate with distant outposts and summon the clans to war. 

## **Dwarf Miner**
Dwarf Miners are the best in the world, with both excellent instincts for locating new finds, and a rugged adaptability to life underground. Their mines are the deepest parts of any Dwarf hold, so encounters with Goblins, Skaven, Trolls, and other monsters are an occupational hazard. 

## **Karak Miner**
When called to war, the warriors of the Miner’s Guild fight as they work — wielding picks, and travelling underground. By swiftly digging new tunnels, they undermine and outmanoeuvre their enemies, surprising foes who expected to fight a static and reactionary battleline. 

Karak Miners replace the 2nd level of the Miner ( **WFRP Core Rulebook** ) Career.

**Trappings** : _Dwarf Pick_ , _Miner’s Helm_ , Davrich 

## **Dwarf Messenger**
The mountains between Karaks belong to enemies of the Dwarfs, so delivering messages from one to another is as perilous as it is essential. For Karak Rangers, who specialise in overland travel, see page 72. For Sky Pilots who deliver messages via gyrocopter, see page 56. 

## **Runebearer**
Runebearers are long-distance runners who deliver vital messages between holds. Though expected to cross any terrain necessary to reach their destination, they specialise in navigating the tunnels of the Underway. Every Runebearer dreams of setting a new record on the Kislev Run, the longest distance ever travelled in a single mission. 

Runebearers replace the 2nd level of the Messenger ( **WFRP Core Rulebook** ) Career.

Lamp, Candle, Lamp Oil, Breastplate, Mail Skirt 

## **Lodefinder**
The elite of the mining clans are known by many names, including Lodefinders and Lodewardens. Their ability to sniff out valuable deposits is legendary, and they are often trusted to drive or operate advanced mining engineering equipment. 

Lodefinders replace the 3rd level of the Miner ( **WFRP Core Rulebook** ) Career.

## **Dwarf Slayer**
## **Slayers Do Not Wear Armour**
Becoming a Slayer is a means of atonement, not a career choice. Dwarfs who lost honour through such acts as oathbreaking, cowardice fighting against traditional Dwarf enemies, or betrayal of the clan can only find redemption through their heroic death against overwhelming odds. 

Slayer Characters cannot ever choose to wear or carry protective wargear. Doing so would risk robbing themselves of the glorious death they crave above all else. More importantly, it would violate their Slayer Oath to Grimnir, mortally dishonouring themselves a second time over, with a shame not even the Slayer Oath can redeem. 

Disgraced Dwarfs journey to the Temple of Grimnir at the nearest Dwarf hold where they undergo the Slayer Ritual ( _Drengidumar_ ). They are stripped of all personal possessions; hair shaved on the heads other than a strip over the crown of their head; remaining hair dyed with a bright, unnatural colour (usually bright orange) in order to distinguish their dishonoured status from afar; hair spiked with animal fat; and ritually tattooed with symbols marking their shame, including Grimnir’s Rune. The would-be Slayer is then inducted into the cult of Grimnir the Slayer. No oath is taken as the oath of a disgraced Dwarf has no value. 

Slayers may change Careers as they acquire new expertise — perhaps studying under Malakai Makaisson to become an Outcast Engineer (page 56), or joining the Slayer-Captain Long Drong’s crew of Pirates ( **Sea of Claws** page 78). But even as the Character changes Career, their Slayer Oath remains binding. They are still oathsworn to forsake shields and armour, even if they acquire them as Trappings from their new Careers. 

If a player is considering playing a Slayer, but finds the ban on wearing armour to be restrictive, frustrating, or an unacceptable constraint on character agency, the solution is simple: play a different Career. There are many Career options, in this book and others, that provide the opportunity to play a powerful, armoured, monster-slaying warrior that should be more in line with their tastes. The Slayer Career provides a more unusual gameplay challenge, in line with their more unusual character perspective. Embrace that challenge only if you are enthusiastic to do so with sincerity! 

The new Slayer may join with other Slayers as shock troops for a Dwarf hold. Most depart their homes and make their way through the manling realms or wilderness to find their redeeming death. 

Slayers tend to avoid other Dwarfs as their company reminds Slayers of what they have lost. Slayers tend to gravitate towards adventuring types who promise danger and chance of honourable death. Dwarf adventurers and Slayers interact with an uncomfortable degree of informality. The two types of Dwarfs can only travel together if there are manlings in the group to afford the Dwarf and Slayer some separation. If a Slayer is forced by circumstance to travel with a group of Dwarfs, the Slayer gloomily accepts such a fate as the will of the Ancestor Gods to add bitterness to the Slayer’s punishment. 

Dwarf attitudes towards Slayers are mixed. On one hand, the words and lives of these disgraced, contemptible outcasts are worthless. On the other, the Slayers’ terrifying ferocity and suicidal bravery command the respect of the warrior-respecting Dwarfs. In addition, the presence of Slayers reminds Dwarfs of how far they can fall if they stray from the values of their culture. 

Slayers forsake membership of clan, guild, and hold, and so fall outside the usual structure of Dwarf society. By convention, their seniority is denoted by the largest, most dangerous monster they’ve slain, but exceptions to this hierarchy are noticeable when a Slayer Army musters at Karak Kadrin. 

## **Brother of Grimnir**
Much speculation and little verified fact determines why the Doom Priests choose to induct a Slayer into the Brotherhood of Grimnir. These experienced Slayers mark their dedication with runic tattoos of warding, and undertake missions sacred to their Ancestor God that they hope will finally kill them. 

Brothers of Grimnir replace the 2nd level of the Slayer ( **WFRP Core Rulebook** ) Career. 

## **Doomseeker**
Loners even by Slayer standards, Doomseekers fasten axes to themselves with locked chains, so they can never forget their obligations to Grimnir. Their vision of a glorious death is to take hundreds of enemies down with them, in rampages so wild they’re a danger to both friend and foe. 

Doomseekers replace the 3rd level of the Slayer ( **WFRP Core Rulebook** ) Career.

War-mourner was once the title of ancient Dwarf champions, who were oathsworn to uphold their king’s honour on his behalf in battle. If a Dwarf were to resurrect the title on behalf of the Slayer King of Karak Kadrin, they could fulfil his Slayer Oath in his stead, ending the cycle that has doomed the Ironfist line.

Dwarf throngs mostly consist of craftsguild labourers, drilled to fight as warriors when conscripted by thane or king. Those most suited to military life are the first drafted for any campaign, supplanting their civilian occupation and effectively transforming them into professional Soldiers. 

## **Axefighter**
Many Dwarfs consider the axe the only fitting weapon for a true warrior, and by long tradition regiments of Dwarfs go to battle carrying axes as their primary weapon, preferring the heft and hitting power of a solid war axe over the finesse of a sword blade.

Crossbows are the traditional Dwarf hunting weapon — more sturdy than bows, and more reliable than blackpowder. Disciplined ranks of Quarrellers have formed the basis of throng firing lines for millennia, standing up far better in melee than most armies’ missile troops.

Beer is serious business in the World’s Edge Mountains. The miracle workers of the Brewing Clans have slowly refined their recipes over generations, pairing the genius of their ancestors with the latest in engineering technology. The resulting concoctions are often volatile to the point of lethal for non-Dwarfs to consume, but an absolute delight for Dwarfs themselves. The most skilled Brewers enjoy a rarified position in Dwarf society, with the most renowned — such as the legendary Josef Bugman — just as celebrated as war heroes and High Kings. 

Like in most craftguilds, an aspiring Brewer begins as an apprentice, where they are kept busy lugging kegs, studying recipes, and testing batches. After years of training, they become Brewers, and eventually acquire enough experience to be considered a Brewmaster. Most of this labour is undertaken in the clan’s breweries, each a fortified structure built to withstand attack by covetous bandits, Goblins, and Giants. If a King takes a particular liking to a Brewmaster’s work, he may send for the Dwarf to serve him as his Chief Victualler, a daunting role that combines the duties of dining butler, head chef, and poison-tester all as one. 

A common Dwarf proverb alleges that beer is best appreciated by those who are most desperate. Perhaps this is why alcohol abuse is so prevalent amongst adventuring parties — and why Brewers are so often found accompanying them. Others join war parties for protection whilst collecting rare ingredients, or use the constant travel as an opportunity to market their goods abroad. Those hungriest for vengeance might be invited to join Bugman’s Rangers, a company of former Brewers whose brewery was destroyed, and who now travel the world visiting fury upon enemies of the Karaz Ankor.

Most Dwarfs do not celebrate war, accepting it as a grim necessity to keep their people safe. Yet they immortalise the heroics of their warrior ancestors, who found glorious deaths in combat. These warrior cults are kept alive by the Doom Priests, bombastic warmongers rarely found far from the frontline. Their stories are an inspiration to Dwarfs seeking to emulate their ancestors’ valorous deeds, Slayers most especially. 

The pre-eminent fighter of the Dwarf pantheon is of course Grimnir, the Ancestor God of war, who disappeared whilst venturing north to seal the great gates of the Realm of Chaos. Many of the most belligerent Clans trace descent from the Slayer God, through his sons Grindol and Morgrim, or their sons Durgin and Gunn. With the exception of Morgrim’s faithful, most of Grimnir’s heirs imitate his furious approach to combat, integrating his personal rune into war tattoos, and charging forward in a berserk rage. Because of this, Doom Priests are easily mistaken for Slayers by nonDwarfs, which is considered a mortal insult. The easiest distinction is that Doom Priests usually wear armour into battle, whilst Slayers would never do so. 

The priesthood of Grimnir rarely have the political responsibilities of Grungni and Valaya’s chosen, leaving them free to tend their war shrines, and accompany Dwarf Warriors on quests or campaigns. They shepherd their kin to glory with horn blasts, runic standards, or by getting stuck in and showing how it’s done. Slayers are especially deserving of their attention, and many Doom Priests provide guidance to these lost souls by tattooing their bodies, accepting their oaths, inducting veterans into the Brotherhood of Grimnir, and pledging to witness their demise.

## **Forge Priest**
_You preserve and restore the oldest examples of Dwarfen craftsmanship to honour the master-builders who preceded you._ 

‘Grome was here, at King Kurgan’s side, when he earned his noble demise.’ — Inscription upon one of the Five Hundred Oathstones of Black Fire Pass 

Naturally, Forge Priests have a vital role in preserving their ancient shrines, whilst a hold’s High Priest of Grungni commonly serves on their King’s council. But there are many circumstances that might justify leaving such duties behind, such as quests to reclaim ancient Dwarf treasures. Other Forge Priests work as custodians of runic items when they are withdrawn from the Dwarfen armoury — bearing a Thane’s arms, for example, or serving as an Anvil Guard in defence of an Anvil of Doom.

## **Forge Priest — Silver 2**
The masterworks forged by the Ancestor Gods are the closest things Dwarfs have to religious relics. Many, such as the Stone of Grungni on the Silver Road, have withstood the passage of time; others, such as the lost Dolmen of the Gods, are surely only waiting to be rediscovered. Forge Priests ensure that these miraculous creations, and their creators, are treated with the veneration they deserve. Their ranks includes the priesthood of Grungni, father and ruler of the Dwarf pantheon, but also devotees of Smednir (Ancestor God of metalworking), Thungni (Ancestor God of runic magic), Morgrim (Ancestor God of engineering), and other ancestors of legendary crafting skill. 

Besides honouring the creations of others, Forge Priests are expected to work a trade themselves. This is partly an expression of faith, but also a practical convenience, so that Forge Priests can restore artefacts that are damaged by enemies or the passage of time. Any attempt to update the designs of the ancients is inherently controversial, so even routine maintenance is an act of great ceremony. Only those serving in the ancestor cults would be permitted such an honour.

Hearth Priests can be found wherever there are Dwarfs that need shelter and medical assistance, which often as not means the frontline. They dress for combat as well as comfort, with enough weapon training to look after themselves. Often they are the glue that keeps a small party together, whether that’s as leader, caregiver, or a mixture of the two.

Valaya is the Ancestor God of hearth and home, protector of her children’s bodies and spirits. Her priesthood, traditionally female, follows her example by providing medical care and reassurance to wounded or ailing Dwarfs. But they do more than simply render assistance to others — Valaya was a governor and trendsetter, the pioneer that founded cities and created rune script, present in her children’s lives whilst Grungni disappeared into his forge, or Grimnir was on campaign. The high priestess of Valaya is a vocal presence in any King’s council, and even the lowliest Hearth Initiate is expected to be forthright and bold, to be worthy of their Ancestor God’s blessing. 

Despite the legendary resilience of Dwarfen physiology, there are some ills that cannot be cured, with tragic consequences. When a Dwarf dies, ceremonies must be observed to usher their spirit to the Hall of the Ancestors. Such rituals are usually observed by the priests of Gazul, or priests of Valaya in holds where the God of the Underworld is not worshipped. Other revered ancestors of Dwarfen domestic culture include Snorri Whitebeard, first High King of the Dwarfs after his father Grungni, and Yinlin the master brewer, whose ales were blessed by Valaya herself.

Hammerers are the red right hand of Thanes and Lords, their most trusted protectors and combat enforcers. In some ways, they are analogous to the Knights of other cultures, albeit with less political or religious obligations. They take their name from the massive, two-handed mallets they wield, a ceremonial gift from their lord in return for undying loyalty. Some claim this choice of weapon honours Kadrin Redmane, an ancient master craftsman, who saved the life of his King armed only with his forge hammer, and was rewarded with a runic greathammer in return. 

A Dwarf may be Oathsworn to another as a mere beardling, usually as part of a political or business exchange between two royal families. More commonly, Hammerers are recruited from within the ranks of experienced Soldiers (page 61), receiving their title by royal appointment after distinguishing themselves in combat. When not accompanying their lord, Hammerers are tasked with guarding their master’s most precious holdings — the gateways to throne rooms, treasure vaults, and the Karak’s main entrance. These duties nurture a suspicious and unwelcoming demeanour, as Gate Keepers prioritise the safety of their charge ahead of social niceties. 

A Hammerer who earns their lord’s trust through illustrious service may be chosen to bear them into battle upon a Shield Platform (page 96). The greatest honour any Hammerer can receive is to carry the ancient Throne of Power, seat of the Dwarfen High King since time immemorial. Only once in history has a Thronebearer ever abandoned in their High King in battle, and the shame of the infamous Forkhelm Shiverback is so severe that no Dwarfs would choose to speak of him 

Because of their dependability, Dwarf lords often instruct Hammerers to take care of any difficult circumstances they can’t attend to themselves. As travelling troubleshooters, Hammerers excel at defending those under their lord’s protection, and solving problems with brute force. More delicate issues are less suited to their capabilities. After all, when all you have is a hammer…

Most holds and roads through the once-great Karaz Ankor have been overrun by malevolent creatures. The Dwarfs bar the gates to their lost dominions, but sometimes a way through must be forced — to seize an opportunity, or escape a greater peril. Ironbreakers form the vanguard of any venture through the underworld, and the first line of defence against underground incursion. Unlike the glorious Hammerer corps, these grim elites must accept that their final stands in the lonely dark are unlikely to be remembered by any besides those fighting at their side. 

A Warrior with plentiful experience battling Night Goblins and Skaven underground might be labelled a Shieldbreaker, receiving extra training to help navigate the tunnels of the Underway. Ironbreakers usually recruit from these formations, choosing the strongest, bravest, and most dutiful Dwarfs. Each Ironbreaker is gifted a gromril suit of armour, a treasured masterwork of impeccable craftsmanship that deflects all but the most determined attacks. When an Ironbreaker falls, their fellows close ranks around them — not just to protect their fallen comrade, but to retrieve their priceless armour. 

**Trappings** : _Gromril Suit_ , Gromril Helm (Closed)

In recent years, the Engineers Guild have developed new Drakefire weapons, to help the Ironbreakers keep pace with the escalating warp-technological insanity of the Skaven. These weapons are effective but volatile, a danger even to the Irondrakes that wield them, who must wear runic gromril to withstand the Drakefire’s heat. 

Where possible, Ironbreakers fight together in tight formations, led by their Ironbeards and Ironwardens. But there are too few Ironbreakers to patrol the whole Underway, and often individual Ironbreakers are dispatched to escort journeys through the dark. When duty leads an Ironbreaker to battle on the surface, they find the skills they honed in brutal subterranean skirmishes are still plenty useful.

**Skills** : Athletics, Climb, Cool, Dodge, Endurance, Melee (Basic), Outdoor Survival, Perception, Ranged (Throwing), _Trade (Cartographer)_ **Talents** : Orientation, Stone Soup, Strider (Any One), Strong Back

## **Karak Ranger — Silver 1**
**Skills** : Consume Alcohol, Melee (Two-handed), Play (Drum _or_ Horn), Ranged (Crossbow), Secret Signs (Ranger), Stealth (Any One) **Talents** : Combat Aware, Demolisher*, Rover, Tireless*

Dwarf Rangers are trackers, explorers, saboteurs, and ambush hunters. They wander far from the borders of the Karaks, keeping a wary eye on approaching (or fleeing) enemies. They provide a vital service to the mountain holds, delivering intelligence on the outside world that could otherwise escape the Karaks’ notice. Despite this, they are often looked down upon by those they protect, dismissed as flighty vagrants without the stomach to put down roots as true Dwarfs should. 

Those destined to become Rangers get their first taste of overland travel by scrabbling across the mountains of their home. From there, an unquenchable wanderlust carries them far beyond mountain ranges, across forests and streams and perhaps even oceans. Whilst Dwarfs are not especially disposed towards speed or stealth, Rangers make up for it with tenacity and resourcefulness. They carry weapons for every occasion, training to battle their enemies at range or up close as required. 

When adventure calls, Dwarf Rangers have few professional or domestic responsibilities they struggle to walk away from. Yet many of the quests Rangers undertake do ultimately serve the home that disrespects them. By their actions are treasures recovered, kinfolk rescued, and grudges satisfied — services rendered to lord and Clan, without expectation of gratitude or acknowledgement.

Though literacy rates amongst Dwarfs are far higher than manlings, only a few are well-educated enough to master the whole Khazalid alphabet. These Runescribes are a precious resource, working as assistants for Thanes, Kings, and other important officials. Others fulfil bureaucratic functions at border crossings, legal disputes, and negotiations, or toil away in the archives of their holds, updating records in the Hall of Remembrance. 

Khazalid symbology is closely entwined with Dwarf history, culture, and technology, and an academic who learns the entire runic script will quickly become expert on a great many specialist subjects. This is fortunate, as Runescribes are expected to keep up whilst their masters reference obscure legal procedures or engineering calculus. Because Dwarfs speak much faster than they can engrave, Runescribes often work from memory, and accusing a Runescribe of faulty recollection is considered a grave offence. 

An exceptional Runescribe may be apprenticed to a Loremaster, taking the title of Lorekeeper whilst undergoing their tutelage. Loremasters are living records of all that is known and remembered by the Dwarfen people, with a breadth of knowledge usually proportional to their age. It is said that Loremasters stay sharp by witnessing as much as they can firsthand, recording great victories and tragedies as objectively as they can… or sending a Runescribe in their stead.

## **Runelord — Gold 4**
The Runesmith clans are the most esoteric and paranoid in Dwarfen culture, guarding their secrets so obsessively that they are never written down, and can only be learned through direct tutorship. This is because their magical craftsmanship is so powerful that it can only be trusted to the most worthy students, lest their power be turned against the Dwarfs. A skilled Runesmith can craft magical items that are the envy of any other culture — weapons, armour, talismans, and more, to suit the needs of their fighting kin. 

After completing a typically gruelling apprenticeship, Runesmiths are permitted to forge whatever runes most speak to them, whilst receiving a generous stipend from their Clan. Runesmiths do not sell their creations, and can rarely be commissioned except by their Kings, so they are rarely guided by practicality. To forge a rune, they might need to seek out a distant mentor, gather bizarre ingredients, or find a one-of-a-kind place of power. These adventures tend to be dangerous, so Runesmiths travel in the company of others, earning their keep by creating runic items and providing magical protection. 

After forging several runes, a Runesmith is ready for the challenge of replicating a master rune. The greatest Runesmiths are known as Runelords, individuals who have crafted multiple master runes, or maybe even invented their own. Some are shockingly ancient, such as Kragg the Grim of Karaz-a-Karak, and are seldom seen outside their forges. Others are (relatively) younger and more intrepid, embarking on quests for lost runic artefacts like Thorek Ironbrow of Karak Azul, or even seeking runic power in the creations of Humans and Elves like Gotri Hammerson of Zhufbar. 

**Skills** : Leadership, Lore (Any) **Talents** : Ancestral Grudge*, Iron Will, Menacing, Pure Soul 

**Trappings** : _Master Runic Wargear_

Thanes are the ruling class of Dwarf society, bowing to none save their Kings. Their honour is inseparable from the Clan they command, obliging them to represent their kin as a respectable authority figure. This includes personally leading their Clan into battle, where they assume the role of officers and generals. The greatest Lords are fearsome warrior commanders, unafraid to get stuck in where the fighting is thickest. 

Most Thanes inherit their title, and those that have inherited recently (or are soon to do so) feel particular pressure to meet the staunch expectations of their peers and subjects. Not every Thane is up to the task. Dwarfs are usually loath to disobey instructions from direct superiors, but a weak, foolhardy, or tyrannical leader brings the whole Clan into disrepute, and every Dwarf has their limit. Thanes considered most successful seek counsel from their advisors, cherish the wisdom of the ancients, trust the skill of their subjects, and prosecute their enemies without mercy. 

Any Thane knows that if you want a job done properly, sometimes you have to take care of it yourself. This goes especially when settling a grudge that is deeply personal, integral to the honour of the Clan, or both. So it is that some Thanes are found wandering far beyond their Clan’s dominions, with only a party of their most loyal retainers for company.
